    Talk to the agent about a printer, where the printers column is
    
    "+ Add printer" on Home opened a modal dialog that ran a fixed recognition
    script against OpenAI, and "Printer settings…" opened OrcaSlicer's own settings
    window. Both now open a conversation in Home's printers column: the Prepare
    screen's panel, with a printer session behind it, so the same agent both adds a
    printer and changes one. Wireframe 19b, decided on turn 19.
    
    The session is its own, not the project's. AgentHost gained four small seams --
    the instructions and tools of the turn, the page messages of a surface, the
    state that surface pins, and the tools it runs -- and the panel supplies all
    four. Its document is an in-memory ProjectPersistence, so nothing said about a
    printer is written into the project that happens to be open, and every opening
    of the panel is a new session with no history carried over.
    
    The agent has four tools here, exposed to this session only: search the
    packaged profiles by the person's own words, draw a printer and fill the pinned
    card, offer up to three specific next actions, and change the printer this
    panel is about. Adding is not one of them: the person taps "Add this printer"
    on the card, and that tap is the approval. Changing a printer does show the
    coordinator's approval card, as every mutation does.
    
    A printer's nozzle moves it onto its model's profile for that size, which is
    the "implemented later" that 6fffcd4703 named when it took the nozzle out of
    the Prepare header. That function is restored here, as a named-printer
    operation, where the panel states the result.
    
    Deleted with the dialog: its controller, its launcher, its own OpenAI
    recognition client, its photo check, their tests and their geometry tokens.
    PrinterCatalog and PrinterDiscovery stay -- the tools read them -- and the
    wizard's "set it up myself" naming behaviour moves to Printers:: intact.
    
    Verification: 152 AgentUI and 45 HomeUI vitest cases, 17 new Catch2 cases for
    the session (including that it writes nothing into the project), the three C++
    suites green, and every state of both flows rendered at the column's real width
    in light and dark through a new preview harness and compared against the
    wireframes on Windows.
    
    No OrcaSlicer-owned file is touched.

    Talk to the agent about a printer, where the printers column is
    
    "+ Add printer" on Home opened a modal dialog that ran a fixed recognition
    script against OpenAI, and "Printer settings…" opened OrcaSlicer's own settings
    window. Both now open a conversation in Home's printers column: the Prepare
    screen's panel, with a printer session behind it, so the same agent both adds a
    printer and changes one. Wireframe 19b, decided on turn 19.
    
    The session is its own, not the project's. AgentHost gained four small seams --
    the instructions and tools of the turn, the page messages of a surface, the
    state that surface pins, and the tools it runs -- and the panel supplies all
    four. Its document is an in-memory ProjectPersistence, so nothing said about a
    printer is written into the project that happens to be open, and every opening
    of the panel is a new session with no history carried over.
    
    The agent has four tools here, exposed to this session only: search the
    packaged profiles by the person's own words, draw a printer and fill the pinned
    card, offer up to three specific next actions, and change the printer this
    panel is about. Adding is not one of them: the person taps "Add this printer"
    on the card, and that tap is the approval. Changing a printer does show the
    coordinator's approval card, as every mutation does.
    
    A printer's nozzle moves it onto its model's profile for that size, which is
    the "implemented later" that 6fffcd4703 named when it took the nozzle out of
    the Prepare header. That function is restored here, as a named-printer
    operation, where the panel states the result.
    
    Deleted with the dialog: its controller, its launcher, its own OpenAI
    recognition client, its photo check, their tests and their geometry tokens.
    PrinterCatalog and PrinterDiscovery stay -- the tools read them -- and the
    wizard's "set it up myself" naming behaviour moves to Printers:: intact.
    
    Verification: 152 AgentUI and 45 HomeUI vitest cases, 17 new Catch2 cases for
    the session (including that it writes nothing into the project), the three C++
    suites green, and every state of both flows rendered at the column's real width
    in light and dark through a new preview harness and compared against the
    wireframes on Windows.
    
    No OrcaSlicer-owned file is touched.
    
    Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

content.text:
**Yes—the setup experience was carried over in code, but the replacement introduced a bug that hides it.**

The history shows:

- **`ae8001553d` — September 13:** embedded Agent Setup inside the old Add printer dialog.
- **`0e55c4f9be` — September 17:** replaced the dialog with the conversation panel. It reused the setup screens and retained the setup-completed callback.
- **`bd81401da2` — September 18:** moved the automatic greeting into the page; the underlying problem remained.
- **`288b9f0dd7` — September 19:** merged that conversation flow.

The bug is in [App.tsx:326](/C:/src/JusPrin/src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/AgentUI/src/App.tsx:326): setup appears only when the agent is unavailable **and the conversation contains zero messages**.

But the printer panel automatically inserts its greeting—even without a configured agent. That makes the message count nonzero, hides setup, and displays the disabled conversation we saw.

This interaction already existed in the September 17 replacement. The printer-panel tests don’t cover an unavailable agent with the automatic greeting.

**So this needs a regression fix, not a new setup experience:** printer setup visibility must depend on agent configuration, rather than whether its greeting exists. No code changed during this investigation.

- If concurrency makes an invalid state reachable, fix the ordering or synchronization instead of suppressing the resulting error.
- Suppress an error only when it is genuinely expected and safely recoverable; document the reason and cover it with a test. Never broadly swallow unexpected errors.
- Prefer removing the root cause over reducing the visibility of its symptoms. Tests should encode valid transitions and assert that invalid ones remain visible.

## Build Commands

```bash
# macOS
cmake --build build/arm64 --config RelWithDebInfo --target all --

# Linux
cmake --build build --config RelWithDebInfo --target all --

# Windows (replace %build_type% with Debug/Release/RelWithDebInfo)
cmake --build . --config %build_type% --target ALL_BUILD -- -m
```

Node/npm is required to build the Agent and Home pages, or configure with `-DJUSPRIN_BUILD_WEB=OFF` and supply the bundles.

## Testing

Catch2 framework. Tests in `tests/` directory.

```bash
cd build && ctest --output-on-failure           # all tests
ctest --test-dir ./tests/libslic3r              # individual suite
ctest --test-dir ./tests/fff_print
```

Printer UI without hardware: `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Testing/README.md` (Bambu in-process fake). Isolated `--datadir`; do not drive another JusPrin instance.

## Code Style

- C++17, selective C++20. PascalCase classes, snake_case functions/variables
- `#pragma once` for headers. Smart pointers and RAII preferred
- Parallelization via TBB — be mindful of shared state

## Key Entry Points

- App startup: `src/OrcaSlicer.cpp`
- Slicing pipeline: `src/libslic3r/Print.cpp`
- All print/printer/material settings: `src/libslic3r/PrintConfig.cpp`
- GUI: `src/slic3r/GUI/`
- Core algorithms: `src/libslic3r/` (GCode/, Fill/, Support/, Geometry/, Format/, Arachne/)
- Printer profiles: `resources/profiles/[manufacturer].json`

## JusPrin Production UI

- Start with `agent-docs/jusprin/README.md` for the canonical product definition, production architecture, verification method, Orca integration guidance, and design system.
- Before editing any file outside `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/`, read `agent-docs/jusprin/fork-stewardship.md`. Every line changed in an OrcaSlicer-owned file is a line this fork re-resolves at every rebase, so those changes must be small, product-neutral, additive where possible, and accompanied by the rebase evidence that document requires.

A value with no token gets a token and a guard first, never a literal.
- Temporary working docs (handoffs, findings, plans written for another agent) stay untracked: never commit them, and never add them to `.gitignore` or `.git/info/exclude`. Untracked files in `git status` are how Kenneth tracks work that isn't finished.

## Critical Constraints

- **Backward compatibility required** for .3mf project files and printer profiles
- **Cross-platform** — all changes must work on Windows, macOS, and Linux
- Profile/format changes need version migration handling
- Dependencies built separately in `deps/build/`, then linked to main app

## Code review focus areas

- Changes must not cause regressions in existing functionality, defaults, profiles, or project compatibility.
- Features gated by options must not affect existing behavior when those options are disabled.
- Changes should follow the existing code style and architecture. Architectural changes should be justified in code comments and the PR description.
- Add helper functions or utilities only when existing code cannot reasonably be reused. Avoid duplication.
- Changes to OrcaSlicer-owned files must be additive where possible. Rewriting an upstream function, or reimplementing upstream behavior beside it, needs explicit justification in the PR description.
- When an upstream line is deleted or relocated, say where it went and what a future rebase must carry into the new home.
- Keep code concise and clear. Manually simplify AI generated bloated codes before review.
- Include targeted tests or documented verification for behavior changes, especially in slicing logic, profiles, formats, and GUI defaults.

# Fork stewardship

**Status:** Required discipline for every change to an upstream-owned file on `jusprin-newui`.

JusPrin is a long-lived fork. Every line it changes in an OrcaSlicer-owned file is a line it re-resolves at every rebase, forever, by a person who was not there when the line was written. The rules below exist to keep that permanent cost small and, where it cannot be small, to keep it visible.

One question generates all of them: **after this change, what does the fork own?**

- Owning a *small neutral seam* is acceptable. It is the kind of thing upstream might plausibly have written itself, so it survives refactors and could be contributed back.
- Owning *upstream's behavior* is the expensive kind. It commits us to re-deriving upstream's intent forever, and the day we take ownership is usually the day the behavior quietly diverges.

Two mechanical facts drive everything else. Unnoticed drift is, and conflicts that resolve wrongly are.

## The ten principles

### 1. Conflict probability is about where you write, not how much

**Rule.** Place fork edits where upstream rarely writes, and keep the number of distinct sites low.

**Mechanism.** Risk is roughly *how often upstream edits this region* times *how much of the region you occupy*, summed over every place you touched. Each site is an independent draw. New files have probability zero, so their size is free; one line inside a function upstream is actively reworking is expensive.

**The test.** How many separate places does this change touch, and how busy is each one? Would one seam deliver the same capability?

**Violation.** Delivering a single capability through a dozen scattered notification lines across several upstream files, when one funnel that every path already passes through would have carried them.

### 2. A clean merge is not a safe merge

**Rule.** Prefer edits that are locally correct over edits that participate in upstream's control flow.

**Mechanism.** Git merges text. If your edit's correctness depends on the code around it — an ordering, a guard, an early return, an invariant nobody wrote down — upstream can restructure the surroundings, the merge succeeds, and your edit now runs under assumptions that no longer hold, with no signal at all.

**The test.** If upstream restructures the code around this hunk, do I get a conflict or silence? If silence, would any test catch it?

**Violation.** Moving a member out of a constructor's initializer list because a callback can fire mid-construction. Nothing in upstream's code records that invariant, so a future cleanup restores the old form with no conflict and no error.

### 3. Add to upstream's code; do not revise it

**Rule.** Append, insert, and call. Do not rewrite upstream functions or change their signatures.

**Mechanism.** An additive hook fails gracefully: when it conflicts, the resolution is "keep both," and anyone can do that correctly. A rewritten function fails badly: every future upstream change to it is a conflict whose resolution requires re-deriving two intents at once, in code no longer shared with upstream. Rewriting subtle logic also tends to change it, and you find out later.

**The test.** Does upstream's line survive my change? If I deleted or replaced one, why could I not have added next to it?

**Violation.** Replacing OrcaSlicer's undo and redo implementations with fork-owned equivalents in order to learn whether the history position moved. Re-expressing the vendor-specific snapshot walk silently dropped one of its branches. An additive helper that reports the result, leaving upstream's functions untouched, would have answered the same question.

### 4. Own the policy; borrow the mechanism

**Rule.** No product name, color, dimension, or product-specific decision in an upstream-owned file. Upstream files may gain small neutral capabilities; the policy that uses them lives in fork-owned code.

**Mechanism.** Product specifics in upstream files are permanent divergence: they can never be upstreamed and never dropped, so they must be re-resolved forever. A neutral capability — a flag, a getter/setter pair, an event — reads like something upstream could have written, which is exactly why it survives refactors.

**The test.** Would this addition look reasonable in an upstream pull request, with no explanation of our product?

**Violation.** A product-named enum value inside a rendering class, or product decisions embedded in an upstream mouse handler. The fix is a neutral options struct plus a fork-owned controller that applies our policy.

### 5. One seam beats many touch points

**Rule.** Find the single place every path already passes through, and put the fork's line there.

**Mechanism.** Each touch point is an independent conflict draw and an independent thing a future resolver must understand. Collapsing many small recurring costs into one is worth some indirection.

**The test.** Do all the paths I am hooking already converge somewhere downstream? Is there one function that runs exactly when the thing I care about has happened?

**Violation.** Publishing a history-changed event from undo, from redo, and from both history-navigation entry points, when all four funnel through a single update function that runs only on a successful move.

### 6. One shared implementation is worth a guaranteed conflict

**Rule.** When the alternative is two copies of the same behavior, keep the shared path and accept that it will conflict.

**Mechanism.** A conflict is a stop; drift between two copies is silent and unbounded. Trading an invisible risk for a visible, small, recurring one is a good trade.

**The test.** Where did the logic I removed actually go? A move has one implementation; only a duplication risks divergence. If I wrote new behavior beside an existing upstream path rather than calling it, upstream's future improvements will never reach our users.

**Violation.** Writing a second object-duplication routine next to OrcaSlicer's clipboard path and pointing an existing dialog at it. Reusing the existing path — extending it where it was too narrow — keeps one implementation.

### 7. Unavoidable conflicts must be easy to resolve correctly

**Rule.** When you must delete or relocate an upstream line, say at the site what moved, where it went, and what a future rebase must carry across.

**Mechanism.** The real cost of a conflict is not the stop; it is the chance of resolving it wrongly. Appending near an upstream line yields a conflict whose obvious resolution — keep both — is right. Deleting an upstream line yields a conflict whose obvious resolution — take mine, the logic moved — silently discards whatever upstream did to that line in the meantime.

**The test.** Six months from now, is the natural resolution of the conflict I am creating the correct one? If not, what does the resolver need to read to get it right, and is that text next to the conflict?

**Violation.** Removing an upstream snapshot label that upstream later localized. Git stops for a human, but the intent-faithful resolution throws the translation away, and nothing at the site says otherwise.

### 8. Do not diverge where you gain nothing; converge where upstream already went

**Rule.** No gratuitous formatting, reordering, or whitespace differences. Before reverting a cosmetic difference, compare against current upstream — it may have made the same change.

**Mechanism.** Every valueless difference is a conflict site that buys nothing. And if upstream has independently arrived at your version, "fixing" it back creates divergence rather than removing it. Adopting a change upstream has already made converges the two trees early and makes the eventual conflict resolve itself.

**The test.** Does this difference carry meaning? Has upstream already made it?

**Violation.** Consuming a shared blank line in a list of build subdirectories, where upstream also appends entries.

### 9. Verify the risk claim instead of reasoning about it

**Rule.** Before asserting that a change is or is not rebase-risky, check it. Three checks, each one command: does git actually conflict there; has upstream already converged on the same change; is the change a move or a duplication.

**Mechanism.** A coherent story about fork risk is not a true one, and every one of these is cheaper to check than to argue about. Reasoning alone reliably produces confident, wrong claims — that a lost change is "silent" when git stops for it, that a move is a "duplication," that a cosmetic difference is gratuitous when upstream shares it.

**The test.** Did I run the simulation, or am I describing what I expect it to say?

**Violation.** A report that lists which files are rebase-sensitive and calls the change narrow, without having run the merge simulation that would have found two lossy resolutions waiting in it.

### 10. Pull direction dominates every local edit

**Rule.** Replay the fork's own commits onto upstream. Never merge upstream in, and never rebase the whole branch.

**Mechanism.** The fork's own footprint is small; the inherited release-branch history is not. Merging upstream in makes the conflict surface the entire divergence between the release branch and upstream's development line — none of it ours. Rebasing only our commits discards that inherited history by taking upstream's version of every file we never touched.

**The test.** Am I replaying our commits onto upstream, or bringing upstream into ours?

**Violation.** `git merge upstream/main`, which produces a conflict list dominated by vendor profiles, translations, and CI files that JusPrin has never edited.

## Before you finish

A change that touches upstream-owned files is not done until this is recorded in the handback or pull request:

1. **The rebase simulation and its result.** Run it against current upstream and name both endpoint commits — measurements are not reproducible otherwise.

   ```bash

   ```

2. **An account of every upstream line deleted or rewritten.** Where the logic went, and why an additive form was not possible.

3. **A statement of what the fork now owns.** Policy, a neutral seam, or upstream behavior. The third needs an explicit justification.

An automatic merge is evidence about today's text. It is not proof that a future rebase will merge, and never proof that the merged result behaves correctly. After every upstream update, run the focused contract tests, the full native build, the real multi-plate workflow, native gizmo input, and the stock-behavior regression checks.

## This fork's terrain

Facts specific to OrcaSlicer, worth knowing before choosing where to put a seam. They change over time; re-measure rather than trusting these.

`Plater.cpp` is by far the busiest file the fork touches, followed by the central `src/slic3r/CMakeLists.txt`, `GLCanvas3D.cpp`, and `PartPlate.cpp`. `GLToolbar` and `GLGizmosManager` are quiet. File-level churn is only a first approximation: some functions inside `Plater.cpp` have not been touched upstream in the entire life of this fork, and a seam there is far cheaper than the file's overall rate suggests. Measure the function, not just the file.

Some native state is shared rather than owned by one object. OrcaSlicer's collapse toolbar belongs to `Plater` and is used by both the Prepare and Preview canvases, so a per-canvas guard cannot save and restore it correctly. Shared state needs one owner at the shared lifetime boundary, and exact restoration needs a getter as well as a setter.

`MainFrame`'s Notebook is cheaper to wrap than to dismantle. Dozens of
upstream predicates — menu and shortcut enabling, `can_delete`, slice status
updates, undo/redo gating — key off `m_tabpanel->GetSelection()`, so removing
or reparenting the Prepare/Preview pages breaks them with no conflict and no
error. A shell gets a tabless full-window layout for free instead: hide the
strip via the public `GetBtnsListCtrl()` (wxBookCtrlBase gives a hidden
controller zero size, so pages fill the client area), and the stock slice and
print side buttons disappear with it because `ButtonsListCtrl` reparents them
into the strip at construction. The Phase 1 production shell reached a
19-added-line upstream footprint this way where the POC's reparenting shell
needed edits across eight upstream files.

The same measurement gives the rule for every fork-owned screen that comes
after the shell. OrcaSlicer's surfaces (the stock homepage, Prepare, Preview,
Monitor, the settings tabs) stay inside the Notebook, because their
correctness depends on it. Fork-owned surfaces (the header, the Agent pane,
Home, and whatever follows) live outside it, as siblings of the Notebook in a
fork-owned sizer, shown and hidden by the shell. The shell *reads* the
Notebook's selection to decide what to show and *never edits its page list*:
no `RemovePage`, `InsertPage`, or reparenting of a stock page. Removing or
replacing a page hands the fork the meaning of that index. Upstream keeps
addressing it by number — `tpHome` as a dialog parent, the target of
`EVT_LOAD_URL`, the tab `post_init` returns to — and every one of those lands
on the fork's widget with no conflict and no error. If a fork surface truly
must be a page, append it last, where no upstream code addresses it.

Navigation between screens stays a Notebook selection change even when the
screen being left is fork-owned. Menu and shortcut enabling, undo and redo
availability, and slice-status updates all read `GetSelection()`, so the
selection must remain the one record of which OrcaSlicer surface is active.
Showing Prepare any other way leaves those predicates answering for the wrong
page, silently.

Some stock behavior is already exposed as an event idiom rather than a
function. Upstream itself drives plate slicing from two places with the same
sequence — the slice button and the Cmd+R shortcut both run
`plater->update(true, true)`, post `EVT_GLTOOLBAR_SLICE_PLATE` to the Plater,
and select the Preview tab — so fork code may repeat that short dispatch
without violating the shared-implementation rule; the behavior itself stays
owned by Plater's event handler.

Historical measurements and the incidents behind several of these rules are in the [OrcaSlicer integration guide](orca-integration-guide.md) and, for the spike era, in the [POC reference](poc-reference.md).
#pragma once

#include <cstdint>
#include <optional>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

namespace Slic3r::GUI::JusPrin::PrinterSetup {

// What a printer is doing, as far as this application can see. Offline is a
// statement about what was observed, not a claim that the machine is off.
enum class PrinterActivity : std::uint8_t { Offline, Idle, Printing };

struct DiscoveredPrinter
{
    std::string stable_id;
    std::string name;
    std::string ip_address;
    std::string device_model_id;
    std::string connection;
    bool connected{false};
    PrinterActivity activity{PrinterActivity::Offline};
    // When the device last said anything, as milliseconds since the epoch.
    // Zero when it never has: a printer known from a previous session but not
    // heard from since is a real state, and a fabricated timestamp is not.
    std::int64_t observed_at_ms{0};
    // What the printer reported about itself; zero or empty when it has not said.
    double nozzle_diameter{0.};
    std::string ams_name;
    struct Spool
    {
        std::string name;
        std::string colour;   // "#RRGGBB"
        std::string material; // the filament type, such as PLA; may be empty
    };
    std::vector<Spool> spools;
    // The machine the app is working with, as Orca's device manager has it.
    bool selected{false};
    // The job in progress; -1 and empty when it has not said.
    int         progress_percent{-1};
    std::string job;
    // Degrees Celsius, as last reported; absent when it has not said.
    std::optional<double> nozzle_temperature;
    std::optional<double> bed_temperature;
};

struct PrinterCandidate
{
    // Opaque, session-local identifier for one model and nozzle variant.
    std::string id;
    std::string vendor_id;
    std::string vendor_name;
    std::string model_id;
    std::string model_name;
    std::string device_model_id;
    std::string variant;
    std::string preset_name;
    std::string build_volume;
    std::string default_material;
    std::string default_plate;
    std::string artwork_path;
};

} // namespace Slic3r::GUI::JusPrin::PrinterSetup

### 1. Conflict probability is about where you write, not how much

**Rule.** Place fork edits where upstream rarely writes, and keep the number of distinct sites low.

**Mechanism.** Risk is roughly *how often upstream edits this region* times *how much of the region you occupy*, summed over every place you touched. Each site is an independent draw. **Violation.** Delivering a single capability through a dozen scattered notification lines across several upstream files, when one funnel that every path already passes through would have carried them.

### 2. A clean merge is not a safe merge

**Rule.** Prefer edits that are locally correct over edits that participate in upstream's control flow.

**Mechanism.** Git merges text. **Rule.** Append, insert, and call. Do not rewrite upstream functions or change their signatures.

**Mechanism.** An additive hook fails gracefully: when it conflicts, the resolution is "keep both," and anyone can do that correctly. One question generates all of them: **after this change, what does the fork own?**

- Owning *product policy* is safe. It is ours, upstream will never write it, and it lives in our files.
- Owning a *small neutral seam* is acceptable. It is the kind of thing upstream might plausibly have written itself, so it survives refactors and could be contributed back.
- Owning *upstream's behavior* is the expensive kind. It commits us to re-deriving upstream's intent forever, and the day we take ownership is usually the day the behavior quietly diverges.

Two mechanical facts drive everything else. Git merges text, not meaning: it conflicts when two sides touch the same or adjacent lines, and it stays silent when they touch different lines even if the result is nonsense. And a conflict is a *stop* — a human is forced to look — while silent divergence is unbounded and invisible. Conflicts are therefore not the enemy. Unnoticed drift is, and conflicts that resolve wrongly are.

## The ten principles

### 1. Conflict probability is about where you write, not how much

**Rule.** Place fork edits where upstream rarely writes, and keep the number of distinct sites low.

**Mechanism.** Risk is roughly *how often upstream edits this region* times *how much of the region you occupy*, summed over every place you touched. Each site is an independent draw. New files have probability zero, so their size is free; one line inside a function upstream is actively reworking is expensive.

**The test.** How many separate places does this change touch, and how busy is each one? Would one seam deliver the same capability?

**Violation.** Delivering a single capability through a dozen scattered notification lines across several upstream files, when one funnel that every path already passes through would have carried them.

### 2. A clean merge is not a safe merge

**Rule.** Prefer edits that are locally correct over edits that participate in upstream's control flow.

**Mechanism.** Git merges text. If your edit's correctness depends on the code around it — an ordering, a guard, an early return, an invariant nobody wrote down — upstream can restructure the surroundings, the merge succeeds, and your edit now runs under assumptions that no longer hold, with no signal at all.

**The test.** If upstream restructures the code around this hunk, do I get a conflict or silence? If silence, would any test catch it?

**Violation.** Moving a member out of a constructor's initializer list because a callback can fire mid-construction. Nothing in upstream's code records that invariant, so a future cleanup restores the old form with no conflict and no error.

### 3. Add to upstream's code; do not revise it

**Rule.** Append, insert, and call. Do not rewrite upstream functions or change their signatures.

**Mechanism.** An additive hook fails gracefully: when it conflicts, the resolution is "keep both," and anyone can do that correctly. A rewritten function fails badly: every future upstream change to it is a conflict whose resolution requires re-deriving two intents at once, in code no longer shared with upstream. Rewriting subtle logic also tends to change it, and you find out later.

**The test.** Does upstream's line survive my change? If I deleted or replaced one, why could I not have added next to it?

**Violation.** Replacing OrcaSlicer's undo and redo implementations with fork-owned equivalents in order to learn whether the history position moved. Re-expressing the vendor-specific snapshot walk silently dropped one of its branches. An additive helper that reports the result, leaving upstream's functions untouched, would have answered the same question.

### 4. Own the policy; borrow the mechanism

**Rule.** No product name, color, dimension, or product-specific decision in an upstream-owned file. Upstream files may gain small neutral capabilities; the policy that uses them lives in fork-owned code.

**Mechanism.** Product specifics in upstream files are permanent divergence: they can never be upstreamed and never dropped, so they must be re-resolved forever. A neutral capability — a flag, a getter/setter pair, an event — reads like something upstream could have written, which is exactly why it survives refactors.

**The test.** Would this addition look reasonable in an upstream pull request, with no explanation of our product?

**Violation.** A product-named enum value inside a rendering class, or product decisions embedded in an upstream mouse handler. The fix is a neutral options struct plus a fork-owned controller that applies our policy.

### 5. One seam beats many touch points

**Rule.** Find the single place every path already passes through, and put the fork's line there.

**Mechanism.** Each touch point is an independent conflict draw and an independent thing a future resolver must understand. Collapsing many small recurring costs into one is worth some indirection.

**The test.** Do all the paths I am hooking already converge somewhere downstream? Is there one function that runs exactly when the thing I care about has happened?

**Violation.** Publishing a history-changed event from undo, from redo, and from both history-navigation entry points, when all four funnel through a single update function that runs only on a successful move.

### 6. One shared implementation is worth a guaranteed conflict

**Rule.** When the alternative is two copies of the same behavior, keep the shared path and accept that it will conflict.

**Mechanism.** A conflict is a stop; drift between two copies is silent and unbounded. Trading an invisible risk for a visible, small, recurring one is a good trade.

**The test.** Where did the logic I removed actually go? A move has one implementation; only a duplication risks divergence. If I wrote new behavior beside an existing upstream path rather than calling it, upstream's future improvements will never reach our users.

**Violation.** Writing a second object-duplication routine next to OrcaSlicer's clipboard path and pointing an existing dialog at it. Reusing the existing path — extending it where it was too narrow — keeps one implementation.

### 7. Unavoidable conflicts must be easy to resolve correctly

**Rule.** When you must delete or relocate an upstream line, say at the site what moved, where it went, and what a future rebase must carry across.

**Mechanism.** The real cost of a conflict is not the stop; it is the chance of resolving it wrongly. Appending near an upstream line yields a conflict whose obvious resolution — keep both — is right. Deleting an upstream line yields a conflict whose obvious resolution — take mine, the logic moved — silently discards whatever upstream did to that line in the meantime.

**The test.** Six months from now, is the natural resolution of the conflict I am creating the correct one? If not, what does the resolver need to read to get it right, and is that text next to the conflict?

**Violation.** Removing an upstream snapshot label that upstream later localized. Git stops for a human, but the intent-faithful resolution throws the translation away, and nothing at the site says otherwise.

### 8. Do not diverge where you gain nothing; converge where upstream already went

**Rule.** No gratuitous formatting, reordering, or whitespace differences. Before reverting a cosmetic difference, compare against current upstream — it may have made the same change.

**Mechanism.** Every valueless difference is a conflict site that buys nothing. And if upstream has independently arrived at your version, "fixing" it back creates divergence rather than removing it. Adopting a change upstream has already made converges the two trees early and makes the eventual conflict resolve itself.

**The test.** Does this difference carry meaning? Has upstream already made it?

**Violation.** Consuming a shared blank line in a list of build subdirectories, where upstream also appends entries.

### 9. Verify the risk claim instead of reasoning about it

**Rule.** Before asserting that a change is or is not rebase-risky, check it. Three checks, each one command: does git actually conflict there; has upstream already converged on the same change; is the change a move or a duplication.

**Mechanism.** A coherent story about fork risk is not a true one, and every one of these is cheaper to check than to argue about. Reasoning alone reliably produces confident, wrong claims — that a lost change is "silent" when git stops for it, that a move is a "duplication," that a cosmetic difference is gratuitous when upstream shares it.

**The test.** Did I run the simulation, or am I describing what I expect it to say?

**Violation.** A report that lists which files are rebase-sensitive and calls the change narrow, without having run the merge simulation that would have found two lossy resolutions waiting in it.

### 10. Pull direction dominates every local edit

**Rule.** Replay the fork's own commits onto upstream. Never merge upstream in, and never rebase the whole branch.

**Mechanism.** The fork's own footprint is small; the inherited release-branch history is not. Merging upstream in makes the conflict surface the entire divergence between the release branch and upstream's development line — none of it ours. Rebasing only our commits discards that inherited history by taking upstream's version of every file we never touched.

**The test.** Am I replaying our commits onto upstream, or bringing upstream into ours?

**Violation.** `git merge upstream/main`, which produces a conflict list dominated by vendor profiles, translations, and CI files that JusPrin has never edited.

## Before you finish

A change that touches upstream-owned files is not done until this is recorded in the handback or pull request:

1. **The rebase simulation and its result.** Run it against current upstream and name both endpoint commits — measurements are not reproducible otherwise.

   ```bash
   git merge-tree --write-tree --merge-base=<fork base> upstream/main HEAD
   ```

   For each conflicted file, state whether the natural resolution is correct or lossy. A lossy one is a defect to fix now, not a note for later.

2. **An account of every upstream line deleted or rewritten.** Where the logic went, and why an additive form was not possible.

3. **A statement of what the fork now owns.** Policy, a neutral seam, or upstream behavior. The third needs an explicit justification.

An automatic merge is evidence about today's text. It is not proof that a future rebase will merge, and never proof that the merged result behaves correctly. After every upstream update, run the focused contract tests, the full native build, the real multi-plate workflow, native gizmo input, and the stock-behavior regression checks.

## This fork's terrain

Facts specific to OrcaSlicer, worth knowing before choosing where to put a seam. They change over time; re-measure rather than trusting these.

`Plater.cpp` is by far the busiest file the fork touches, followed by the central `src/slic3r/CMakeLists.txt`, `GLCanvas3D.cpp`, and `PartPlate.cpp`. `GLToolbar` and `GLGizmosManager` are quiet. File-level churn is only a first approximation: some functions inside `Plater.cpp` have not been touched upstream in the entire life of this fork, and a seam there is far cheaper than the file's overall rate suggests. Measure the function, not just the file.

Some native state is shared rather than owned by one object. OrcaSlicer's collapse toolbar belongs to `Plater` and is used by both the Prepare and Preview canvases, so a per-canvas guard cannot save and restore it correctly. Shared state needs one owner at the shared lifetime boundary, and exact restoration needs a getter as well as a setter.

`MainFrame`'s Notebook is cheaper to wrap than to dismantle. Dozens of
upstream predicates — menu and shortcut enabling, `can_delete`, slice status
updates, undo/redo gating — key off `m_tabpanel->GetSelection()`, so removing
or reparenting the Prepare/Preview pages breaks them with no conflict and no
error. A shell gets a tabless full-window layout for free instead: hide the
strip via the public `GetBtnsListCtrl()` (wxBookCtrlBase gives a hidden
controller zero size, so pages fill the client area), and the stock slice and
print side buttons disappear with it because `ButtonsListCtrl` reparents them
into the strip at construction. The Phase 1 production shell reached a
19-added-line upstream footprint this way where the POC's reparenting shell
needed edits across eight upstream files.

The same measurement gives the rule for every fork-owned screen that comes
after the shell. OrcaSlicer's surfaces (the stock homepage, Prepare, Preview,
Monitor, the settings tabs) stay inside the Notebook, because their
correctness depends on it. Fork-owned surfaces (the header, the Agent pane,
Home, and whatever follows) live outside it, as siblings of the Notebook in a
fork-owned sizer, shown and hidden by the shell. The shell *reads* the
Notebook's selection to decide what to show and *never edits its page list*:
no `RemovePage`, `InsertPage`, or reparenting of a stock page. Removing or
replacing a page hands the fork the meaning of that index. Upstream keeps
addressing it by number — `tpHome` as a dialog parent, the target of
`EVT_LOAD_URL`, the tab `post_init` returns to — and every one of those lands
on the fork's widget with no conflict and no error. If a fork surface truly
must be a page, append it last, where no upstream code addresses it.

Navigation between screens stays a Notebook selection change even when the
screen being left is fork-owned. Menu and shortcut enabling, undo and redo
availability, and slice-status updates all read `GetSelection()`, so the
selection must remain the one record of which OrcaSlicer surface is active.
Showing Prepare any other way leaves those predicates answering for the wrong
page, silently.

Some stock behavior is already exposed as an event idiom rather than a
function. Upstream itself drives plate slicing from two places with the same
sequence — the slice button and the Cmd+R shortcut both run
`plater->update(true, true)`, post `EVT_GLTOOLBAR_SLICE_PLATE` to the Plater,
and select the Preview tab — so fork code may repeat that short dispatch
without violating the shared-implementation rule; the behavior itself stays
owned by Plater's event handler.

Historical measurements and the incidents behind several of these rules are in the [OrcaSlicer integration guide](orca-integration-guide.md) and, for the spike era, in the [POC reference](poc-reference.md).

#include <cstdint>
#include <optional>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

namespace Slic3r::GUI::JusPrin::PrinterSetup {

// What a printer is doing, as far as this application can see. Offline is a
// statement about what was observed, not a claim that the machine is off.
enum class PrinterActivity : std::uint8_t { Offline, Idle, Printing };

struct DiscoveredPrinter
{
    std::string stable_id;
    std::string name;
    std::string ip_address;
    std::string device_model_id;
    std::string connection;
    bool connected{false};
    PrinterActivity activity{PrinterActivity::Offline};
    // When the device last said anything, as milliseconds since the epoch.
    // Zero when it never has: a printer known from a previous session but not
    // heard from since is a real state, and a fabricated timestamp is not.
    std::int64_t observed_at_ms{0};
    // What the printer reported about itself; zero or empty when it has not said.
    double nozzle_diameter{0.};
    std::string ams_name;
    struct Spool
    {
        std::string name;
        std::string colour;   // "#RRGGBB"
        std::string material; // the filament type, such as PLA; may be empty
    };
    std::vector<Spool> spools;
    // The machine the app is working with, as Orca's device manager has it.
    bool selected{false};
    // The job in progress; -1 and empty when it has not said.
    int         progress_percent{-1};
    std::string job;
    // Degrees Celsius, as last reported; absent when it has not said.
    std::optional<double> nozzle_temperature;
    std::optional<double> bed_temperature;
};

struct PrinterCandidate
{
    // Opaque, session-local identifier for one model and nozzle variant.
    std::string id;
    std::string vendor_id;
    std::string vendor_name;
    std::string model_id;
    std::string model_name;
    std::string device_model_id;
    std::string variant;
    std::string preset_name;
    std::string build_volume;
    std::string default_material;
    std::string default_plate;
    std::string artwork_path;
};

} // namespace Slic3r::GUI::JusPrin::PrinterSetup
"}

+# Handoff: adding printer settings versus connecting a physical printer

+Date: 2026-09-22. Working baseline: `b361b84773e8a7978f0ea6491a2e9ef7725b73fc` plus the current uncommitted AgentUI changes described below.

+## User request and intended outcome

+Neither the assisted add-printer screen nor the manual printer-selection screen clearly explains whether the user is adding settings or connecting a physical machine. A new user reasonably asks: “Will this find my printer on Wi-Fi? Can I print after this?”
+
+Explain what adding a printer accomplishes, then present connection as a separate, optional step. The user's main concern is feasibility: understand how OrcaSlicer's existing mechanisms fit together before designing or implementing a new flow. This is an investigation-first handoff, not a request to rewrite Orca's printer subsystem.

+The next agent should produce an evidence-backed architecture map, a capability matrix, and a bounded implementation recommendation. Separate confirmed behavior, inference, and unresolved questions. If assigned implementation afterward, use that recommendation to deliver small, independently verifiable changes.

+## Read first and preserve current work

Verify retry/idempotency behavior rather than assuming duplicates always occur or never occur.

+### Current flow, simplified

+```text
+Assisted choice -> AddPrinterRequest
+  -> install/select system preset
+  -> save named user preset (+ optional Bambu device link)
+  -> optional access-code write
+  -> one success/error result -> conversation closes or shows error

+Stock host settings -> PrintHost provider -> provider-specific test/send path
+```
+
+The missing piece is not just explanatory text: the product needs an honest outcome contract and a way to connect an already saved printer without adding it again.
+
+## Feasibility investigation: answer these before choosing an implementation

clearly distinguishes adding printer settings from connecting a physical printer -   Is it from the app developers point of view or users point of view?

“Adding printer settings” is mostly the **developer’s point of view**. Users think, “I want to use my printer,” not “I want to create a profile.”

The distinction matters, but we should explain it through what the user can do:

- **Add your printer:** “Choose your printer so JusPrin can prepare prints for it.”
- **Connect your printer — optional:** “Send prints directly to your printer. You can set this up later.”

After adding it, say **“Your printer has been added”**, followed by the optional connection step—not “Printer settings added.”

So the UX should distinguish the **outcomes**, without teaching users Orca’s internal separation between profiles and devices.

# Handoff: adding printer settings versus connecting a physical printer

Date: 2026-09-22. Working baseline: `b361b84773e8a7978f0ea6491a2e9ef7725b73fc` plus the current uncommitted AgentUI changes described below.

**Temporary working document. Keep this file and any follow-up investigation documents untracked. Do not commit them or add ignore rules.**

## User request and intended outcome

Neither the assisted add-printer screen nor the manual printer-selection screen clearly explains whether the user is adding settings or connecting a physical machine. A new user reasonably asks: “Will this find my printer on Wi-Fi? Can I print after this?”

Explain what adding a printer accomplishes, then present connection as a separate, optional step. The user's main concern is feasibility: understand how OrcaSlicer's existing mechanisms fit together before designing or implementing a new flow. This is an investigation-first handoff, not a request to rewrite Orca's printer subsystem.

The next agent should produce an evidence-backed architecture map, a capability matrix, and a bounded implementation recommendation. Separate confirmed behavior, inference, and unresolved questions. If assigned implementation afterward, use that recommendation to deliver small, independently verifiable changes.

## Read first and preserve current work

Start at `agent-docs/jusprin/README.md`, then read the product definition, architecture, engineering method, Orca integration guide, fork stewardship, and design system it links. Follow repository `AGENTS.md` instructions.

The current worktree contains unrelated/pending work that must be preserved:

- The startup wizard suppression is already committed at the baseline above.
- Uncommitted changes in `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/AgentUI/src/App.tsx`, `PrinterPanelApp.test.tsx`, `components/Panels.tsx`, and `styles.css` restore the agent-configuration screen during add-printer chat and expose the manual alternative below it.
- That alternative reads “Not ready to set up the agent?” with an underlined “Add your printer manually” action. It opens the existing stock printer-selection wizard. Its screenshot is `UX-audit-current-20260921/manual-printer-fallback.png`. It was presented for user review; do not treat this handoff as approval to commit it.
- Existing audit directories and `wizard-startup-verification.md` are untracked evidence. Preserve them.

There are **three different concepts** to keep separate in the product language: configuring the AI agent, saving printer settings, and connecting a physical printer. An unavailable AI agent must not block the latter two workflows.

## What the code establishes today

Locations below are investigation entry points, not permission to change every file. Line numbers are approximate; locate the named functions in the current checkout.

| Responsibility | Existing owner / entry point | Confirmed behavior and implication |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Catalog and add/change contract | `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/PrinterSetup/PrinterBackend.hpp` | `AddPrinterRequest` combines model/profile choices with optional device ID and access code. The interface exposes add/change and manual setup, but no explicit connect-an-existing-printer operation. |
| Install settings and save a named printer | `PrinterSetup/OrcaPrinterBackend.cpp`, `add_printer` (~107) | Installs/selects the system preset, saves a named user profile, then optionally handles an access code. Saving and connection are already sequential operations, although the return contract does not represent their separate outcomes. |
| Named printer identity and persistence | `Printers/NamedPrinters.hpp` and `.cpp` under `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/` | A JusPrin named printer is an Orca user printer profile. Writes reuse upstream preset operations. A separate app-config mapping links Bambu device ID to profile name. A previously linked device selects its existing profile; otherwise names can acquire `(2)` suffixes. Do not introduce a second printer database. |
| Manual route | `PrinterSetup/OrcaPrinterBackend.cpp`, `run_manual_setup` (~196) | Runs `ConfigWizard::SP_PRINTERS`; after success, names newly installed models through `name_installed_printers`. Cancellation returns without naming. The method returns `void`, so callers do not receive a structured list of additions or a cancellation result. |
| Conversation completion | `PrinterSetup/PrinterConversation.cpp`, `manual_setup` (~690), `add_proposed_printer` (~719) | Assisted add treats a nonempty backend error as failure and keeps the panel open; success closes through the host. The returned `SavedPrinter added` does not become a detailed save/connection receipt. Manual completion similarly needs tracing before attaching a success screen. |
| Discovered device snapshot | `PrinterSetup/PrinterDiscovery.cpp`, `discover_printers` (~54) | Reads `DeviceManager::get_my_machine_list()`. This is not evidence of a universal Wi-Fi scan. Determine which local/cloud devices enter that list before labeling it “Found on your network.” |
| Access-code handling | `Shell/SetupCommands.cpp`, `set_printer_access_code` (~336) | Validates characters, resolves the machine, and calls `MachineObject::set_user_access_code`. Returning true does not demonstrate authentication or a live connection. |
| Credential setter | `src/slic3r/GUI/DeviceManager.cpp`, `MachineObject::set_user_access_code` (~437); default argument in `.hpp` | Sets the machine field, writes app config, and updates the local-machine record under its existing conditions. This function does not wait for a successful connection. Trace the subsequent owner of connection initiation and confirmation. |
| Existing connection affordance gap | `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Shell/PrinterMenu.cpp` (~73) | Explicitly notes that “Connect…” is deferred. Do not assume a complete connect-later action already exists behind a missing button. |
| Current connection summary | `Shell/SetupCommands.cpp`, `printer_connection` | Uses Bambu networking and the globally selected machine. Other host types return `NotConnected` here; that is not proof those hosts are unreachable. |
| Home cards and navigation | `Home/OrcaHomeBackend.cpp`; `HomeUI/src/components/PrinterCard.tsx`; `HomeUI/src/App.tsx` | Joins named profiles to device records and renders connection/activity/added-printer feedback. Monitor navigation resolves a linked device ID. Inspect all consumers before changing the meaning of a status. |
| Other printer connection mechanisms | `src/slic3r/GUI/PhysicalPrinterDialog.cpp`, `build_printhost_settings`; `src/slic3r/Utils/PrintHost.cpp`, `get_print_host` | The stock host-settings route supports host type/address, authentication, browse/test operations, and provider-specific behavior. It is a different path from Bambu DeviceManager integration. Reuse it where appropriate rather than generalizing the Bambu access-code flow to all printers. |

Paths abbreviated in the middle rows are relative to `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/`.

### Two concrete contract problems to investigate first

1. **A saved printer can be reported as a failed add.** `OrcaPrinterBackend::add_printer` saves the named profile before attempting the access-code step. If that step fails, it fills `added` but returns an error string. The conversation treats that error as a failed add. Design an explicit partial-success outcome: the saved printer remains available; connection can be retried against that same printer. Verify retry/idempotency behavior rather than assuming duplicates always occur or never occur.
2. **“Connected” currently conflates different observations.** `discover_printers` initializes `DiscoveredPrinter.connected` with `machine->is_online() || machine->is_connected()`, while activity uses `is_connected()` alone. The field order is confirmed in `PrinterSetupTypes.hpp`. Trace downstream labels before deciding whether to rename a field, introduce a richer observation, or change presentation. Merely storing credentials, seeing a device online, or selecting a profile must not produce an unqualified successful-connection message.

### Current flow, simplified

```text
Assisted choice -> AddPrinterRequest
  -> install/select system preset
  -> save named user preset (+ optional Bambu device link)
  -> optional access-code write
  -> one success/error result -> conversation closes or shows error

Manual choice -> stock ConfigWizard (printer profiles)
  -> name newly enabled models -> conversation closes

DeviceManager observations -> discovery snapshots -> linked Home/card status
Stock host settings -> PrintHost provider -> provider-specific test/send path
```

The missing piece is not just explanatory text: the product needs an honest outcome contract and a way to connect an already saved printer without adding it again.

## Feasibility investigation: answer these before choosing an implementation

1. **Trace one complete path per connection family.** Start with Bambu LAN, Bambu account/cloud, and a representative generic print host (for example an existing Moonraker or OctoPrint adapter). Identify discovery, credentials, persistence, connection initiation, success/failure observation, selection, restart, and send/monitor entry points. Use `ConnectPrinter.cpp`, `SelectMachine.cpp`, `SelectMachinePop.cpp`, `DeviceManager`, `PhysicalPrinterDialog`, and `PrintHost` as leads. Record which APIs can be reused from fork-owned code and which are dialog-bound.
2. **Separate identities.** Map catalog model, system preset, user preset/name, Bambu device ID, host address, selected slicing preset, and selected monitor machine. Which relationships are durable? What happens on rename, deletion, nozzle-profile change, or two printers of the same model? Verify the `NamedPrinters.hpp` description of upstream profile ownership against actual load/save paths; do not assume a dormant class is the authoritative owner.
3. **Determine actual capabilities.** For each connection family, record whether discovery, address entry, authentication, file upload, start-print, live status, and monitor navigation are supported. “Connected,” “can send a file,” and “ready to start printing” are different claims. Mark unknown/unobserved status honestly. A host that supports upload without continuous monitoring must not appear broken just because no Bambu machine exists.
4. **Find the connect-later boundary.** Can existing dialogs/APIs configure the chosen saved printer without changing an unrelated current project or creating another profile? Can a discovered device be linked to an existing manually added profile? How are incompatible model/nozzle choices handled? What new narrow adapter operation is actually necessary?
5. **Follow asynchronous ownership.** Identify callback threads, object lifetimes, cancellation, timeout/retry, and how a closed panel or changed selected printer affects results. A late event must update the correct saved printer, not whichever profile is now selected. Follow existing synchronization; do not hide invalid transitions behind catch-all errors.
6. **Trace completion on the manual route.** The wizard may add several models, cancel, or enable an already available model. Determine how to identify exactly what was saved before offering a connection step. Do not show “Printer added” merely because the dialog closed.
7. **Check prerequisites and failure states.** Identify network-plugin availability, account/region requirements, LAN/cloud mode restrictions, offline operation, and authentication errors for the supported providers. Do not extrapolate from a fake device or the existence of a settings field.

Deliver a compact matrix with these columns: connection family, existing mechanism, persisted identity/config, observable success signal, supported actions, unresolved gaps, proposed seam, and validation evidence. Estimate effort/risk per slice after this trace, not from the number of UI controls.

**Initial assessment, not a completed feasibility verdict:** profile-only addition is already supported. Clearer explanation and a separate saved-printer receipt appear feasible within fork-owned surfaces. Reliable connect-later behavior is plausible because upstream has connection mechanisms, but the reusable entry points, identity transitions, and provider-specific status contracts still need verification. A universal connection wizard is not yet justified.

## Proposed UX direction to evaluate

Keep the initial task recognizable as “Add printer,” but explain its immediate outcome near both the assistant and the manual choice:

> Add your printer's settings so JusPrin can prepare prints for your model. You can connect the printer afterward.

After a confirmed save, show the printer name/model and a separate optional connection section:

> **Printer settings added**
>
> You can now prepare prints for [printer name].
>
> **Connect your printer (optional)**
>
> Connect to send files directly from JusPrin. You can do this later.
>
> **Connect printer** · **Not now**

This is candidate wording, not a frozen design. Only promise direct sending when the identified provider supports it. Mention file export where the model's workflow supports it. If connection is already verified, show that actual result instead of asking the user to connect again. If settings were saved but connection failed, say so explicitly and retry only connection.

Offer a persistent “Connect printer” action on the saved printer's card/details so “Not now” is a viable choice. Where support is unavailable, explain the supported next action instead of presenting a dead button. Do not use “Ready to print” as a synonym for saved settings, stored credentials, or a network handshake.

Assisted and manual routes should converge on the same saved-printer meaning and later connection route. Keep the stock profile wizard intact where possible; a fork-owned explanation before it and accurate receipt after it may be sufficient. Assess layout and outcome handling before changing upstream wizard screens.

Represent profile-save outcome and connection state separately. A provisional connection vocabulary might include not configured, connecting, verified, failed, unavailable, and status unknown; use only states the underlying provider can support. Distinguish a previously configured device that is currently offline from one never configured. Avoid inventing a universal live-session state machine where a provider only offers request-based tests.

## Implementation boundaries and expected handback

Prefer three bounded slices: (1) explain and report settings-save outcomes accurately, (2) connect an existing saved printer through one proven provider path, (3) extend capability/status handling to other supported families. Document limitations rather than treating the first provider as universal.

- Keep UX, copy, and presentation in the existing web pages; native adapters own Orca state, persistence, invariants, and async lifetimes.
- Reuse `NamedPrinters`, preset operations, DeviceManager, and PrintHost mechanisms. Avoid duplicate authentication, discovery, or configuration stores.
- Keep access codes/API keys out of agent prompts, conversation history, screenshots, and logs. Existing conversation tests already check that only the existence of a supplied access code is recorded.
- Preserve upstream dirty-state behavior. The current add backend only re-baselines an initially clean project with no saved project file; a loaded project's printer change must remain a real edit.
- No broad cleanup of Orca code as a prerequisite. If an upstream seam is necessary, keep it neutral and additive and explain why existing entry points cannot serve. Apply the exact rebase-simulation and ownership evidence requirements in `agent-docs/jusprin/fork-stewardship.md`.
- Use the existing theme tokens and control recipes for any UI implementation. Do not commit this handoff, screenshots, logs, or experimental documents.

The investigation handback should contain: verified call/persistence map; capability matrix; named unresolved questions; a proposed outcome/state contract; smallest implementation plan with ownership and risk; and tests that would establish the claimed behavior. Cite source symbols and distinguish static code inspection from observed runtime behavior.

## Verification and acceptance criteria for subsequent implementation

| Scenario | Required result |
| --- | --- |
| New user, agent unavailable, no printer online | Can choose manually and save settings; no implication of Wi-Fi discovery or successful connection. |
| Assisted and manual completion | Accurate receipt for actual additions, including multiple additions; cancellation does not manufacture success. |
| Skip optional connection | Saved printer survives restart and remains usable for supported preparation/export; connect-later action remains discoverable. |
| Link a manually added printer later | Reuses that saved printer; no accidental second profile; validates model/device compatibility. |
| Bad credentials, disappeared device, or connection timeout | Saved settings remain intact; reason and retry action describe connection failure, not a lost printer. |
| Device online but not authenticated; credentials merely stored | No false successful-connection label. |
| Previously configured printer offline; host without live status | Clear distinction between offline, not configured, and unknown/unavailable observation. |
| Two printers of same model; rename/remove/nozzle change | Stable association with the intended device/config; unrelated printer and project untouched. |
| Close panel, retry, or switch printer during connection | No stale callback, duplicate save, lifetime error, or result assigned to another printer. |
| Existing clean saved project, dirty project, fresh unsaved project | Correct preset selection and dirty-state behavior; no lost save prompt. |
| Supported Bambu and generic host paths | Claims about discovery, authentication, send, and monitor backed by each provider's real behavior. |

Use focused backend/conversation tests (`tests/agent/test_printer_conversation.cpp`), page tests in AgentUI/HomeUI, and the relevant native shell integration coverage (`tests/shell/shell_harness.cpp`). Verify actual adapters, not only mocks. Build affected native/web targets and run applicable theme guards if UI changes.

For hardware-free UI checks, follow `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Testing/README.md` and use an isolated `--datadir`. The in-process Bambu fake can demonstrate UI observations and transitions; it **cannot** establish real discovery, network authentication, pairing, or reconnect behavior. The Moonraker simulator is documented on `jusprin-newui-fakeprinter`; do not assume it exists in this checkout or import it wholesale. State unavailable hardware/provider coverage explicitly. No physical print or heating is needed to evaluate this UX.

Capture both starting routes, successful settings save with optional connection, skipped connection on Home, and connection-failure recovery. Evaluate wording and keyboard/focus behavior from a first-time user's perspective. Keep evidence untracked and show the implemented screens to the user for design review when that implementation is requested.
